clue.text: They are often lit up outside pubs

definitions.text: They are often lit up outside pubs

blocks.note: surface reading: things illuminated, like signs or lamps hung outside a pub

blocks.clueFragment: They are often lit up outside pubs
blocks.note: setter's reading: people who 'light up' a cigarette, banished to the pavement since indoor bans

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lit up' suggests pub signs or fairy lights; read it as 'light up', the phrase for starting a cigarette, and the clue describes the drinkers standing outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Since indoor smoking bans, people who use cigarettes must stand on the pavement beside the pub to indulge.

clue.text: Superstar provides heavenly bread stuffed with delicious olive tips

indicators.note: a tip is the very end of something, so each word gives up its first letter
something stuffed has a filling pushed inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: manna is the food sent from heaven to the Israelites in Exodus
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A celebrity's catering rider: fancy bread filled with nice olives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly bread' sounds like a bakery boast, but it is the food that fell from the sky in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Madonna is the globally famous pop singer, a textbook example of a music superstar.

clue.text: Jack, who doffs his cap in church space

indicators.note: doffing a cap means taking off what sits on top, so the leading letter is removed

blocks.note: the Jack's own top letter, the one he takes off; it is silent anyway
the nave is the main central area of a church where the congregation sits

explanation.surface: A man politely raises his hat on entering a church.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: take the answer, remove its first letter, and the church space is left. So KNAVE is K plus NAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: In a pack of cards the Jack is also called the Knave, the older name for that court card.

clue.text: Cheers after Charlie's appearance in extravagant production by Italians

indicators.note: to make an appearance in something is to turn up inside it
coming after places a piece at the end, behind the rest

blocks.note: a riot (of colour, say) is an extravagant, lavish display
Charlie is the code word for the letter C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
ta is informal British for thanks, as is cheers

explanation.surface: A toast after a celebrity's turn in a lavish Italian show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Production by Italians' looks like opera or film, but it is a food product. 'Cheers' here means thanks, not a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Ricotta is a soft whey cheese made in Italy, so it is literally something Italians produce.

clue.text: 'Howl!' — poem recited as a series of lines

indicators.note: reciting is speaking out loud, so we go by how the words sound

blocks.note: a dog's howl or bark; said quickly before the next word its last sound joins it
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Allen Ginsberg's famous poem Howl being read out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Howl' is a famous Ginsberg poem, which tempts you to keep it whole; it is just a dog's noise. BARK ODE run together sounds like BAR CODE.
explanation.definitionFit: A barcode is a machine-readable pattern of parallel stripes printed on products for scanning at tills.

clue.text: Occasionally call out men, big old boys

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens only every so often, so we keep every other letter

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of these words

explanation.surface: Now and then someone calls out to a group of hefty former pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big' looks like it describes the old boys, but it supplies the final letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Alumni are former students of a school or college, which is what 'old boys' means in British usage.

clue.text: We sold cat spraying fluid produced when frightened

indicators.note: spraying scatters droplets all over, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: We sold the cat because it kept marking the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat spraying fits the pet story perfectly, which hides that 'spraying' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold sweat is the clammy perspiration that breaks out on the skin in moments of fear or panic.

clue.text: Waste long time in prison

blocks.note: dung is animal waste, manure
an eon is an immensely long period

explanation.surface: Wasting years behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste' reads as a verb, but it is the noun for manure.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is a dark underground cell in a castle where captives were kept, a kind of jail.

clue.text: Come upon fatty spread — something I don't fancy

indicators.note: spreading something pushes its parts out of place, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Finding a greasy spread on the table that you would rather not eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fatty spread' reads as one thing, like lard or dripping, but 'spread' is the signal and the fodder ends at 'fatty'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something outside your taste or liking, which is exactly what you don't fancy.

clue.text: Doctrine kids read endlessly

indicators.note: with no ends means both the first and last letters are dropped, leaving only the middle

blocks.note: the inner two letters of this word
the inner two letters of this word

explanation.surface: Children reading on and on about some teaching or creed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' applies to both words, trimming each at the front and back.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctrine is a principle or belief held as true, and an idea can mean such a notion or conviction.

clue.text: Enrich soul performing a stage routine

indicators.note: performing can mean acting up or putting on a turn, so the letters do something different

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Performing in a show feeds the spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Performing' fits the theatre picture so well that it does not look like a signal. The answer also recalls the musical A Chorus Line.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorus line is a row of dancers performing a synchronised number together on stage in a show.

clue.text: Fly home with religious group?

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
a sect is a breakaway religious body

explanation.surface: Taking a flight back to join a religious community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' reads as a verb, travel by plane; it is the noun for a buzzing creature. The question mark flags that a fly is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A fly is one example of an insect, a six-legged creature, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: Common man takes on popular politician

indicators.note: taking something on means taking it aboard, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: mister is the ordinary title for a man with no rank or honour
something in is fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: An ordinary voter confronts a well-liked politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common man' means an untitled man, a plain mister rather than a lord; IN goes after the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A government minister is a politician in charge of a department, so the term names a kind of politician.

clue.text: Risk of obesity is low apparently

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase meaning a low likelihood

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: the chance of getting fat
second meaning: the idiom means very little chance at all, despite sounding large

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like reassuring medical advice; the joke is that the idiom says the opposite of its words, a big-sounding chance that is in fact tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: The sarcastic idiom means practically no likelihood, while read literally the words describe the probability of becoming overweight.

clue.text: Burning everything around motorway

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: creation is the whole universe, everything that exists
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: A blaze consuming everything along a stretch of motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: British motorways are numbered with M, so M stands for motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: Cremation is the burning of a dead body to ashes, so the noun is a specific kind of burning.

clue.text: Process essential to commence expansion

definitions.note: describes the answer rather than replacing it: money is needed to start growing

blocks.note: first meaning: a method or way of doing something
second meaning: money or resources, which any business needs before it can grow

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like business jargon about a growth plan. The second half is a description of the word's other sense, financial resources.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a method used to reach an end and the wealth or capital that allows one to act.

clue.text: Conduct from addict injecting heroin

indicators.note: injecting puts a substance inside the body, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: a user is a drug addict
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: The behaviour of someone shooting up heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conduct' looks like a noun meaning behaviour, but it is the verb, to lead someone somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher someone is to guide them to their seat or place, which is a way of conducting them.

clue.text: Fighter disposing of both sides creates classic record

indicators.note: getting rid of both sides strips the outer letters, front and back

blocks.note: an oldie is a classic song from years ago

explanation.surface: A boxer who ditches both corners and turns out a classic hit.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: strip the answer of its first and last letters and the classic record is what remains, so S and R wrap OLDIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier is a member of an army, someone whose job is to fight in combat.

clue.text: Sweet picture, perhaps added by discrete software module

indicators.note: adding by something sets it alongside, so the pieces are placed side by side

blocks.note: an applet is a small self-contained program
a picture is one example of art

explanation.surface: A cute image bundled with a self-contained piece of code.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' reads as an adjective describing the picture, but it is the British noun for a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a sweet is a dessert course, and a fruit-filled pastry is a classic pudding.

clue.text: Arranged denial without asking first

indicators.note: arranging items puts them in a new order, so these letters are reordered
without means lacking, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of this word, which is removed
up means first in turn, as in 'you're up first'

explanation.surface: Someone set up a flat refusal without being asked beforehand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' does double duty as the definition and the signal to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: To have lined things up is to have organised or set them out in order, a close synonym.

clue.text: Waves used to make other waves

blocks.note: first meaning: long heavy waves rolling in from the sea
second meaning: curlers wound into hair to set it in waves

explanation.walkthrough: The second half sounds like physics or an ocean wave machine; the 'other waves' are in hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both big ocean swells and the cylinders that curl hair into a wavy style.

clue.text: Try uplifting sign given by an enormous number

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting upwards makes the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to have a go is to have a try
a logo is an emblem or sign

explanation.surface: Have a go at an inspirational sign shown by a huge crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' looks like praise for the sign; in a down clue it turns the word upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A googol is ten to the power one hundred, a famously huge figure that inspired the Google name.

clue.text: Repay debt in full and move on

blocks.note: first meaning: to settle an amount owed completely
second meaning: to go away, often told to someone unwelcome

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one financial instruction, but it splits into two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both paying off what is owed and leaving a place when told to go.

clue.text: Plant found in back parts of Thanet Castle

indicators.note: the back part of a word is its tail, so only its closing letters are kept

blocks.note: the final three letters of this place name
the final three letters of this word

explanation.surface: A weed growing behind a castle on the Kent coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Thanet is a district at the north-east tip of Kent, England; only its last three letters matter here.
explanation.definitionFit: The nettle is a common stinging weed, a wild green plant found across Britain.

clue.text: Took the test again after returning a shocker

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: resat is the past tense of resit, to take an exam again

explanation.surface: A student retakes an exam after coming back with an awful result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shocker' suggests a terrible exam result; here it is literal, a device that delivers an electric shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A Taser is a stun gun that fires barbs carrying an electric current, so it literally shocks people.

clue.text: Way to earn money spent moving bodies

blocks.note: a living is the work you do to support yourself
spent means exhausted or used up, finished

explanation.surface: A job that pays you to shift corpses, like a removals firm for undertakers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving bodies' suggests carrying corpses; it means bodies that move by themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Zombies are corpses walking about, so the horror term names bodies that move despite being deceased.

clue.text: Bias shown by some key economic world leaders

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so each word supplies its opening letter

blocks.note: the initial letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Prejudice displayed by certain major figures in the global economy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'World leaders' reads as heads of state; the leaders are the first letters of the four words before.
explanation.definitionFit: A skew is a slant or distortion away from neutral, which is what a bias amounts to.

clue.text: Places to go that are wildly insular

indicators.note: doing something wildly means doing it without control, so the order is thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Holiday destinations that are extremely isolated islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Places to go' sounds like travel destinations; 'go' is the euphemism for relieving yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: A urinal is a fixture in a gents' toilet, and 'go' is a polite way of saying urinate.

clue.text: Most economical spring break

blocks.note: a spa is a mineral spring
a rest is a break from work

explanation.surface: The cheapest holiday deal in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring break' reads as a student holiday; the spring is a mineral water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare means frugal or meagre, so its superlative describes the leanest, most thrifty option.
